thread.title: A Buyable Dip In Cognex? - Cognex Corporation (NASDAQ:CGNX)

author: Stephen Simpson, CFA
title: A Buyable Dip In Cognex? - Cognex Corporation (NASDAQ:CGNX)
text:
Being a value-oriented investor who loves technology, particularly industrial technology, often has me feeling like a stranger in a strange land. There’s never any shortage of “you can’t worry about valuation; you just have to buy!” comments, and it can indeed be frustrating to watch the expensive shares of great companies get ever more expensive and float up and away like a kid’s balloon.
But with great valuation often comes great volatility, and that can work for patient investors. Cognex ( CGNX ) is back where it was when I last wrote about the company , but I believe the company is a little better today, even if its near-term revenue growth opportunities are not. Although the risk of further declines in consumer electronics can’t be ruled out, nor declines in auto spending or issues in China, the valuation now looks close to reasonable and that may be about the best you can hope for, though I’d note the shares are not cheap by most metrics.
It’s Been An Interesting Year… After I wrote about Cognex a little more than a year ago, the shares began a great six-month upward march as strong semiconductor, auto, and consumer electronics orders combined to drive exceptional revenue growth (up 76% in Q3’17) beyond prior sell-side expectations. Cognex’s main rival Keyence ( OTCPK:KYCCF ) benefited from similar trends, and both companies enjoyed strong performance through the end of November.
Since late November, though, Cognex shares have lost about a third of their value (while Keyence has been mostly flat). First quarter performance in 2018 wasn’t bad, with revenue up 17% in constant currency terms, but management flagged a sharp slowdown in consumer electronics spending, that will likely see this major revenue contributor (roughly 40% of revenue) fall by 15% to 20% in 2018 versus a 60% rise in 2017.
There’s nothing fundamentally wrong with Cognex’s business, and I don’t believe the company is losing any meaningful share to Keyence, SICK, or others. Rather, Cognex is another company suffering for its significant business dealings with Apple ( AAPL ) and the sharp correction in demand tied to recent disappointing iPhone sales trends. Unfortunately for Cognex, this is very nearly a “ship on order” company, so management doesn’t have all that much visibility into long-term demand on a customer-specific basis.
The Opportunity Is Still Growing While 2018 isn’t going to be the year that the bulls hoped for with Cognex, I believe the company continues to improve itself and I believe the market continues to develop in attractive ways.
Cognex has spent the last few years building up its capabilities in 3D machine vision, a market that is still relatively small (because it’s new) but offers exceptional growth potential given. Just as 2D machine vision opened the door to considerable automation and mass production for items that once had to be assembled in slower, labor-intensive, multi-step processes, 3D vision can enable the automation of even more complex assembly tasks, not to mention automating several logistics and warehousing tasks.
What has taken place in 3D vision is consistent with Cognex’s “fast follower” approach. Keyence dominates the market today, but it’s a large (likely $500M-plus) fast-growing market that is only just getting started. What’s more, Cognex has built a well-rounded portfolio of 3D solutions including laser profiling, stereo imaging, and structured light, whereas as Keyence uses laser profiling. Only SICK offers similar diversity (though SICK offers time of flight and not structured light), and I wouldn’t be surprised if Cognex bought its way into time of flight at some point, just to round out its offerings.
Meanwhile, the market opportunity itself continues to grow. Machine vision is increasingly not just an enabling technology for factory and warehouse automation, but a gating technology as well. Machine vision is essential to robotics (and Cognex works with four of the five largest players) and I believe it is well on its way to becoming essential in large-scale warehousing.
It’s Not All Beer And Skittles… There are some “but’s” here, though. First, Cognex has a meaningful presence in China (the market leader), and the recent escalations in the trade issues between the U.S. and China won’t help the company. Along those lines, the Chinese government has been actively encouraging local companies in the automation sector, and I believe it’s only a matter of time before there are truly viable and competitive Chinese machine vision companies in the market.
Second, consumer electronics capex spending is demonstrably volatile. While there are still plenty of growth opportunities (including expanding OLED production), it injects added volatility to the story. Third, I believe the strong contributions from auto OEMs (double-digit growth) are likely to slow, though U.S. automakers and Chinese automakers appear to have not yet adopted the technology with the same gusto as their European and Japanese peers and could still be a source of future growth.
I’m also still concerned about overall valuation issues. Most (if not all) of the sell-side sets their price targets on Cognex on the basis of PE multiples and what the market is currently willing to pay for other industrial tech/growth stories. Multiples have certainly expanded over the last couple of years and when the next correction comes, that could hammer those short-term peer-based targets.
The Opportunity Why am I more bullish on a stock that is trading at almost the same price as a year ago? When using discounted cash flow models for fast-growing, relatively small companies, a year can make a lot of difference as the free cash flow Cognex produced in 2017 is less than a third of what I expect for 2027. I’ve also done a lot more research in industrial automation over the past year, and I’m even more confident about the central role machine vision will play in facilitating industrial and logistics automation, and Cognex’s likelihood of remaining a key player.
I believe my expectations are still quite bullish and perhaps aggressively so. I’m modeling double-digit long-term revenue growth and mid-teens long-term FCF growth. I am expecting FCF margins to improve about seven points relative to the company’s long-term trailing average. Although Keyence’s operating margins would suggest significant margin expansion potential for Cognex, I believe the entrance of lower-priced Chinese competitors will cap some of the long-term margin leverage.
The Bottom Line Cognex shares aren’t actually below my DCF-based fair value, nor do they look reasonably-priced (let alone cheap) on what I consider to be a fair forward EBITDA multiple (mid-teens). Nevertheless, I do think the cash flows offer investors a high single-digit annualized return at this price. That’s not what I normally like to see for new investments, but I don’t believe Cognex will get truly cheap unless the company seriously fumbles a few quarters, its end-markets contract suddenly and dramatically, and/or the overall market goes into the tank. Any of those could still happen, and this is by no means a low-risk, conservative call, but seeing the shares close to what I believe is a reasonable valuation gives me an itchy trigger-finger.
